cases.name: Angela Johnson Summers
cases.about:
Her Find-a-Grave said, "Angela Johnson Summers was born Angela Johnson in Indianapolis September 19, 1974 to Harry and Bonnie Johnson.

The family soon moved to an old little Bargersville farmhouse after they added another child, Douglas. Her early years were spent doing a lot of reading, feeding the cows they raised for food, avoiding the rooster who lived in a trash can on the front porch, and helping her mom out in the little floral shop next to the house.

Her dad was really the one who she bonded the with most. He worked as a machinist on Indy’s south side and championed his daughter at school and home. Academically, she was a straight-A student with occasionally perfect attendance, top five in her graduating class at Franklin High School "Class of ‘93", and a James Millikin Scholar for three years at Millikin University where she studied English until ’96.

Angela’s beloved father passed when she was 19, and the loss weighed heavily on her for many years. Also, in ’96, she moved to Indianapolis with her future spouse, Melanie Davis, and they had many adventures there with old friends from Angela’s high school years and new friends who were mostly misfits and artists and others who knew how to have a good time. She and Melanie were married in October of ’99. More adventures were had. In 2005, she gave birth at home to their child, Katrina Davis. The couple split in 2008.

Angela’s primary goal was to find a family to belong to, people she could nourish and who could nourish her. She wound up finding that in three particular places. Teleunique, a fundraising/box office service for non-profits was one of the environments she flourished in. The people there were a family, and they buoyed her in many ways.

Then, at a Thanksgiving event with Katrina, she met some folks from Unity of Indianapolis Church who they connected with. She attended a service, then became a Sunday School teacher, drawing on her upbringing in a more traditional church, and before too long had run for and joined the board. She invested herself with a signature passion that she had for all causes she believed in, and she had found a richly accepting and supportive family at Unity where her life had impacted so many, as well.

Professionally, like many English majors, she struggled to find a good fit. She started a pet treats company with her long-time friend, Melissa Cummings, called Missy’s Morsels and through that and much volunteering for local animal welfare organizations, satisfied her love of taking care of animals. But then she happened upon a career with the Postal Service as a mail carrier, another family where she sought service as a local steward for their union. She was a welcome presence on her route, making friends with the people and animals in her area, passing out treats and smiles and mail, too. She wrote that this was finally a place she felt at home, and her world was coming together in so many ways. It combined family and service and had all the lovely rules and procedures and things she absolutely loved in things like copy-editing, for example.

Then, on April 27, 2020, the bright arc of Angela’s life met the impenetrable wall of senseless violence when she was killed, delivering mail during a pandemic as an essential worker serving her community at risk to herself. She made a couple of prophetic posts on Facebook just hours before she was gunned down four blocks from her own front door. Her death has reverberated across the country on the news, but what those headlines and videos miss is the life she lived. For those who knew and loved her, her entire 45 year stay with us is the story."

cases.name: Marianne Carol Weis
cases.about:
Marianne’s older sister (Susie DeLoach) said: “Our Mari was a beautiful soul who loved to dance and sing.  She lived with a lot of pain, for reasons we’ll keep private. We don’t know much about what happened yet, but seeing her light dimmed this way is devastating.”

Weis had five children and worked as a bartender, server and hairdresser. 

When they were kids, Susie DeLoach and her younger sister used to make up dances together. “We were best friends,” DeLoach said. “As we got older, we kind of gained different interests and had different lifestyles, but she is and will always be a big part of my heart.”  “She had challenges, but everyone has challenges in their life,” DeLoach said. “It's awful the way she was taken from us.” 

DeLoach remembers how her sister liked to dance, ride motorcycles with her father and was a hard worker. While preparing for the funeral, DeLoach has thought about the last concert she and Weis went to together.  

It was a Pat Benatar show in Nashville, Indiana, during the summer of 2023, but the sisters enjoyed all kinds of music together. “I never thought that would be our last one,” DeLoach said.  

From her teenager years at Warren Central High School and beyond, Weis never knew a stranger, her sister said.  

"She finally trusted the wrong person,” DeLoach said. “She was super trusting of people her whole life.” 

Her obituary said, "She graduated from Warren Central High School; class of 1989. Marianne was a talented licensed Cosmetologist. Professionally, she worked as a hairdresser and bartender.

In her leisure time, Marianne often painted, designed jewelery and created art through woodburning. She enjoyed dancing, singing, cooking and riding behind her dad on his Harley Davidson motorcycle. Marianne also enjoyed attending art festivals, nature photography, and spending time with loved ones. She cherished God, her family and dogs. Marianne took great pleasure in being outdoors; whether she was fishing or growing vegetables and flowers, Marianne always found happiness in nature. She loved making new friends, lilacs, fashion and indulging in delicious foods.

Everyone will remember Marianne as funny, sweet, playful, hardworking, compassionate, resourceful and strong. She will be deeply missed by her loving family and friends."

The first thing anyone mentions is how her beautiful smile lit up the room. Jeri didn’t know a stranger; she would smile and start a conversation with anyone around her. Jeri loved her family and friends fiercely. She was the person you would want in your corner, as she would do everything for those she cared about. If she didn’t know you, and you needed help of any kind, she would be the first to offer to find a way to help. Outside of spending time with family and friends, Jeri enjoyed her job, various side jobs, shopping and finding a great deal, going to amusement parks, and spending time at the movie theaters with her children."
